title: Congo's Ebola Death Toll Crosses 1,000 as Experts Warn Outbreak Is Far From Over
excerpt: The Bundibugyo strain outbreak — the fastest-growing in Ebola history — has now killed over 1,000 in the DRC, with no approved vaccine available and armed conflict hampering the response.
body:
• Ebola has killed more than 1,033 people in the Democratic Republic of Congo, with confirmed cases reaching 2,536 as of July 23.
  • The outbreak, caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain, has no approved vaccine or treatment — experimental options are being fast-tracked.
  • Armed conflict in eastern Congo, attacks on health facilities, and conspiracy theories are severely hampering containment efforts.
  • Uganda has contained its cases to 20, with no new infections since June 21, prompting Africa CDC to urge the US to lift travel restrictions.

The Ebola outbreak tearing through the Democratic Republic of Congo has now killed more than 1,000 people, official figures confirmed on Wednesday, as health workers battle a disease with no approved treatment in one of the world's most unstable regions.

Congo's public health institute reported that confirmed cases have climbed to 2,536, with deaths reaching 1,033. In the latest daily update alone, 63 new cases and 34 deaths were recorded, according to Reuters.

The Fastest-Growing Outbreak on Record

Health authorities have described this as the fastest-spreading Ebola outbreak ever recorded. The 2013–2016 West Africa epidemic — which ultimately killed more than 11,000 people — took roughly eight months to reach 1,000 deaths. The current outbreak, declared on May 15, has reached that grim milestone in just over two months.

https://x.com/addisstandard/status/2080527315491053673

The virus is the Bundibugyo strain, which carries a fatality rate of up to 40%. Unlike the more common Zaire strain, there are no approved vaccines or specific treatments for Bundibugyo, making this outbreak uniquely difficult to fight.

"The outbreak has been reported in five provinces, but the province of Ituri remains the epicentre, accounting for more than 90 per cent of cases and 80 per cent of deaths."

— Dr. Thierno Baldé, WHO Incident Manager

Beyond Ituri, the virus has spread to North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uele, and Tshopo. About 80 percent of newly reported infections are linked to unknown transmission chains, indicating the virus is spreading faster than health teams can trace, according to Congo's Ministry of Health.

Conflict, Conspiracy Theories, and Clinic Attacks

Eastern Congo's chronic instability has turned the outbreak response into a logistical nightmare. Dozens of armed groups operate across the region, and attacks on health facilities have forced aid workers to suspend operations in certain areas. Some healthcare workers have gone on strike over unpaid salaries since the outbreak began.

Bereaved families, angered by health restrictions that prevent them from burying loved ones through traditional funeral practices, have clashed with response teams. Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected people — including the dead — making safe burial protocols essential but deeply controversial.

Conspiracy theories alleging the outbreak is a hoax have further complicated community engagement, eroding trust in health workers on the ground.

Children Bearing a Devastating Toll

The human cost extends far beyond the death count. Save the Children reported on July 22 that at least 189 children have died, with 476 children confirmed infected — accounting for over 20% of all confirmed deaths. More than 4,000 children in Ituri are receiving mental health and psychosocial support through safe spaces set up by the organization.

Staff on the ground say the disease has changed how children interact, with many now avoiding close contact and keeping their distance from adults. Anxiety is widespread over whether schools will be able to reopen in September as new cases continue to emerge.

A Race for Experimental Treatments

With no approved treatment available, the scientific community is scrambling. The World Health Organization is prioritizing several experimental drugs — including antibodies, antivirals, and vaccines — to combat the Bundibugyo virus. The University of Oxford has launched clinical trials, and Africa CDC plans to seek rapid ethical approval for a study combining the licensed Zaire-strain vaccine Ervebo with an experimental Sudan Ebola vaccine developed by IAVI.

"Something is better than nothing and we know that it's safe. It is your choice."

— Armand Sprecher, Epidemiologist, Médecins Sans Frontières

Speaking from Bunia, the capital of Ituri province, MSF's Sprecher noted that 35 health workers have been infected and 14 have died. He argued the decision to receive a partially protective vaccine should rest with individual healthcare workers after informed consent. Africa CDC is also discussing contributing an initial $500,000 to launch the vaccine study while seeking additional funding from partners.

The WHO has cautioned against broader deployment of Ervebo outside controlled research settings, warning that breakthrough infections could "generate a false sense of security" and undermine public trust in vaccination efforts.

What It Means for the Indian Diaspora

India has significant economic and diplomatic ties to Central and East Africa, with sizable Indian communities in Uganda, Kenya, and surrounding countries. The US travel restrictions on Uganda — which Africa CDC is now urging Washington to lift, citing no new cases since June 21 — could affect transit routes for Indian professionals and business travellers in the region. India's own public health apparatus will be watching the experimental vaccine efforts closely, given the country's role as a major vaccine manufacturer.

What to Watch

Uganda has entered its 42-day countdown to being declared Ebola-free, with all 836 identified contacts having completed their monitoring period. But in Congo, the outlook remains dire. The WHO sees early signs of stabilization in some areas, but insecurity, unknown transmission chains, and the absence of proven medical countermeasures mean the outbreak could continue to escalate. The coming weeks will test whether experimental treatments can be deployed fast enough to bend the curve.
